39.0.0.en: 1 "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? 2 Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? 3 They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones, they cast out their sorrows. 4 Their young ones come to maturity, they grow up in the wilderness; they go forth, and return not unto them.

39.0.1.en: Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? [1].

39.0.2.en: Most of mankind is not occupied with the wild animals that roam the desert or the forests, but what occupies it is its own work and its own animals, such as flocks, horses, dogs, cats, etc. But God, the Creator of all, cares even for the animals of the wilderness, for their preservation, their bearing of young, their food and drink and their dens.

39.0.3.en: When a man and his wife realize that the wife has become pregnant, they are concerned to know the time of the birth and to observe the labor. And they often turn to specialist doctors to follow the pregnancy until the birth takes place. Thus the birth of a child costs man much care and material expense and psychological and financial preparation; so who cares for the wild goats and hinds when they are pregnant? God Himself tends them and cares for them; will He not then care for man, His beloved creature, so very dear to Him?

39.0.4.en: We can say, after the example of the Apostle Paul who said: "Doth God take care for oxen?" (1 Cor 9:9), [Doth God take care for the bringing forth of the wild goats and the labor of the hinds?] Yes, He is concerned with the human wild goats and hinds who work by His Holy Spirit, and strive to bring forth souls for the Lord. They strike with their feet the heads of serpents to kill them, and each puts its head on the other, and all work together for the gaining of every soul for the Kingdom of God. Then the spiritual teacher sings with the Apostle Paul, saying: "For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor 4:15). "I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Phlm 1:10).

39.0.5.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation of the conception of the wild goats and hinds.

39.0.6.en: * It is the custom of the hinds (the females) to kill the serpents they find, and the serpents try to bite their feet. It is said that when crossing rivers each of them rests her head on the hind in front of her, and so does not feel the weight of her head. Why was Job asked about the bringing forth of the wild goats and hinds, unless because they refer to the character of the spiritual leaders?

39.0.7.en: For they are truly like the wild goats that bear young among the rocks, because through the teachings of the Fathers, who are called rocks, they bring forth souls by their guidance... It was said by Jeremiah of the teachers who in negligence leave the children born to them: "Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it" (Jer 14:5).

39.0.8.en: They are like the hinds who live by destroying sins, that is, dead serpents, and by destroying their sins they burn all the more with longing for the fountain of life. Therefore the psalmist says: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God" (Ps 42:1).

39.0.9.en: It is as though it were said to Job: You think that you are working on a high level, yet you have not known beforehand the time in which the spiritual masters are sent into the world to bring forth children by the teaching of the early Fathers, and by their striving gather for me the souls that are won.

39.1.0.en: Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? [2].

39.1.1.en: Man is not concerned with counting the months that the wild animals complete while pregnant, nor does he care about the time of birth, and even if he were concerned, he would not know the exact time of the birth.

39.1.2.en: If man is ignorant of these things that surround him on the earth he inhabits, does he think he is able to comprehend what is in the mind of God and in His heart? Can he comprehend God's plan toward him and the extent of His love for him?

39.1.3.en: They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones.

39.2.1.en: The birth of the young of wild animals is hard, and no man helps them, yet their young are born safe through God's care for them, and they forget their weariness and pains.

39.2.2.en: The birth of children, especially in advanced countries, takes enormous effort, whether at the level of states or families or individuals, and costs the world much. But the birth of wild animals costs almost no one anything.

39.2.3.en: For the animals "rise early and bring forth their young ones. They cast out their sorrows."

39.2.4.en: May the spiritual teachers trust in the wonderful work of God who works through them to bring forth sons for Him in the Gospel through the riches of God's free grace!

39.2.5.en: * When the saints think of the progress of their hearers, they come into a state of conception, as in the womb. For I present one among many who resembles the hinds, Paul, who speaks like one roaring from the intensity of the pain of labor. He says: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (Gal 4:19).

39.2.7.en: Their young ones come to maturity.

39.2.8.en: They grow up in the wilderness.

39.3.0.en: They go forth, and return not unto them [4].

39.3.1.en: The young of the wild animals soon reach maturity, that is, they grow. For the young of wild animals, or of most animals in general, need no long time nor anyone to teach them suckling and walking and movement, etc. Unlike man, who needs a long period of training to learn to walk and to depend on himself. It is a wonderful divine gift for the animal as for man. The animal needs no one to teach it, because its mother is unable to arrange that, but man needs someone to teach him and a long period in which, while he learns to walk and the manner of eating, etc., he absorbs from the family many customs, enjoys a collective culture, and benefits from the experience of those before him! God has set everything in wisdom, both for the animal and for man!

39.3.2.en: "They go forth, and return not unto them": the young of animals go out after a short time to seek their own food, and do not remain a burden on their mothers. But for human beings it continues for years extending to tens, the family supporting him until he completes his practical studies or his training for a certain profession and becomes independent of his parents.

39.4.0.en: 5 "Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? 6 Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling. 7 He laugheth at the multitude of the village. Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. 8 The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing.

39.4.1.en: Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? [5]

39.4.2.en: Some of the Fathers see in the onager and the wild ass, which frolic in the wilderness without hindrance, symbols of those who walk in the life of solitude in the freedom of the Spirit.

39.4.3.en: * The wild ass that dwells in solitude means the life of those who dwell far from the press of people. It is fittingly said "free" also, because the toil of worldly conduct is great, the mind is confused by it, even if its labors are acceptable to them. To be freed from this state of bondage it is necessary to desire nothing in this world. For men seek after riches, and the enemy presses with a kind of terrible yoke of bondage.

39.4.4.en: But he who frees the neck of his mind from the dominion of temporal desires enjoys a kind of freedom in this life... The Lord saw this heavy yoke when He said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28)... For the Lord looses the bands of the wild ass when He tears from the mind of His chosen ones the fetters of weak dangers, and in His mercy tears to pieces all that binds their brilliant thought.

39.4.6.en: * The wilderness is the mother of stillness, it is the calm and the harbor that saves us from all troubles.

39.4.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * The mere sight of the wasteland gives the soul stillness, and kills in us the passions of the body.

39.4.8.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * Abba Mark said: "This is the reason why stillness is good: that a man does not see in it what is harmful to his soul, and the thing that is not seen does not reach the soul, and what is not in the soul does not stir up in it the memory of sights nor make the passions (that is, the inclinations of the soul) rise up in it, and a man enjoys within himself a deep calm and a manifold peace [or delights in the abundance of peace (Ps 37:11)]".

39.4.9.en: * An elder was asked: "Why did Abba Anthony say to Abba Paul his disciple: Go and dwell in silence until you receive the temptations of the demons?" The elder said: "Because perfection comes to the monk from spiritual conduct, and spiritual conduct arises from the inclinations of the heart, and purity of heart comes from the inclinations of thought, and the manner of thinking is built upon unceasing prayer and the struggle with demons. But unceasing prayer and the struggle with demons, whether in thoughts or in visions, have no opportunity to exist without stillness and solitude".

39.4.10.en: * A brother asked Abba Cronius: "What shall I do to cure the forgetfulness (or negligence) that enslaves my spirit, since before I perceive anything I am led into sin?" The elder said to him: "When the strangers seized the ark of the covenant because of the sins of the children of Israel, they took it to the house of their god Dagon, and then Dagon fell to the ground" (1 Sam 5). The brother said: "What does this mean?" The father said to him: "If the demons try to capture a man's spirit by their own means, they push him so as to lead him to an unknown hidden passion (that is, an inclination of the soul), and here if his spirit returns to seeking God and remembers the eternal judgment, the passion is driven out at once and disappears. It is written: In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isa 30:15).

39.5.0.en: The Garden of the Monks Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling [6].

39.5.1.en: The tame ass is often shut up in a stable inside the field or the house, not moving in it, but the wild ass finds freedom of movement so that it counts the wilderness its own house, and dwells in a suitable region.

39.5.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that for him who practices the life of solitude and stillness the whole desert becomes his house, he moves in it in safety and tranquility, and dwells even in the salt places that inflame man with thirst, so that he is ever hungering and thirsting for fellowship with the Lord.

39.5.3.en: * [Whose house I have made the wasteland, and the salt land his dwelling (tent)]... Those who live in isolation, that is, those who are freed from bodily passions, dwell in stillness of heart, just as the Lord gave the wilderness as a house to the wild ass, so that the crowds of bodily passions do not press upon him...

39.5.4.en: Saltiness suits the burning of thirst, so since the saints live in the dwellings of this life (that of stillness of heart), and burn with the daily warmth of their longing for the heavenly city, it is said that they make their dwellings in the salt land. They are burning with thirst continually, as it is written: [Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled].

39.5.6.en: * Of this number of the perfect, or, if I may call them so, the tree of the saints that has budded and brought forth blossoms and fruits, are the "ascetics"...

39.5.7.en: The Lord spoke of them with Job in a symbolic way, saying: "Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling. He laugheth at the multitude of the village. Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing" (Job 5:39-8). The book of Psalms also says: "Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy" then continues saying: "They wandered in the wilderness in a waste where there was no way. They found no city to dwell in. Hungry and thirsty also, their soul fainted in them. Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses" (Ps 2:107, 4-6). Jeremiah also describes them, saying: "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him" (Lam 27:3, 28). And the words of the psalmist come from the heart: "I am like an owl of the ruins. I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top" (Ps 6:102, 7).

39.5.8.en: Father Piamun He laugheth at the multitude of the village.

39.6.0.en: Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver [7].

39.6.1.en: The wild ass laughs at the multitude of the village when they try to catch him and surround him, for he quickly slips from their hands. "Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver," for he is not like the tame ass which fears the wrath of him who drives it, being exposed to beating. The wild ass feels that he is in a happier state than the tame ass.

39.6.2.en: If we take the symbolic interpretation of Pope Gregory (the Great), who says that the wild ass refers to those who walk the way of stillness and solitude, then these cannot be shut up by the crowds in narrow concepts, nor can any desire or sin drive him according to its whim.

39.7.0.en: The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing [8].

39.7.1.en: He who walks in the spirit of true stillness lives as in a circle of holy mountains, seeking the heavenly pasture.

39.7.2.en: * The mountains of pasture are also the heavenly powers of the angels, since they support us by their ministry to us and their help... We can also take the mountains of pasture to be the lofty sayings of Holy Scripture, of which the psalmist says: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats" (Ps 104:18). For those who know how to practice the leaps of contemplation ascend the high peaks...

39.7.3.en: "And he searcheth after every green thing," for he truly dries up all the things that take shape for a time and wither and lose the sweetness of the present life.

39.8.0.en: 9 "Will the wild ox be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? 10 Canst thou bind the wild ox with his band in the furrow? or will he harrow the valleys after thee? 11 Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him? 12 Wilt thou trust him that he will bring in thy seed, and gather it into thy threshing floor?

39.8.1.en: Will the wild ox be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? [9]

39.8.2.en: "The wild ox," in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great), is the rhinoceros, and he sees that it refers to the pride of this world or the powers of its evil kingdom which destroy men with a spirit of pride. The believer does not expect the powers of evil to serve him, nor does he lodge at his crib, where the word of God is as food for the soul. Pride destroys the believer and does not build him, and corrupts his understanding of the word of God, so that his depths are not satisfied by it.

39.8.3.en: * The rhinoceros is often understood as pride, as we have been taught by the testimony of the prophet who says: [I said unto the boasters (the wicked), Do not boast (do no evil), and to the sinners, lift not up the horn] (Ps 75:4). To what then does the rhinoceros refer but to the power of this world or the very powers of darkness belonging to its kingdom, who exalt themselves in the pride of vain arrogance...

39.8.4.en: Here it is rightly said to the blessed Job, as a representative of the holy Church: [Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee? or abide by thy crib?] By the crib here is understood Holy Scripture itself, upon which the holy animals feed with the food of the word, of whom it was said by the prophet: "Thy congregation hath dwelt therein" (Ps 68:10). Therefore our Lord also, when He was born, was found by the shepherds in a manger, because His incarnation, which refreshes us, we recognize in the Scripture of the prophets.

39.8.6.en: Since Job thought he was able to subdue everything to his will, God said to him: {Begin with the rhinoceros, show me your intelligence and your power, can you make the rhinoceros a tame animal that serves you instead of the animals you lost of camels and donkeys? Show me your power: can you make this animal approach your crib, and eat of the food you used to provide?} Canst thou bind the wild ox with his band in the furrow (Canst thou bind the wild ox with a rope to the line of the plow?)

39.9.0.en: Or will he harrow the valleys after thee? [10]

39.9.1.en: It is as if He says to him: If you cannot use the rhinoceros instead of camels and donkeys, can you use it instead of oxen, binding it to the plow to till the land (the furrow is the line of the plow)?

39.10.0.en: Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him? [11]

39.10.1.en: The rhinoceros as a wild animal is stronger than the donkey and the ox, so can man replace his donkey or his ox with a rhinoceros to serve him?

39.10.2.en: It befits man to realize that if he has lost the service of the wild beasts, it is only because of his sin, for since he rebelled against God these animals rebelled against him. And if the tame animals submit to him and serve him, that is only from God's mercies upon him and His love.

39.10.3.en: Some see that most of the tame animals that serve man are in general weaker than the wild ones. It is as though dealing with man deprives the animal of its strength and ability. In a symbolic story a tiger was amazed when it saw a cat bearing its same form, but small of body and weak. It asked it the secret of its great weakness. The cat answered: Living with man has humbled me and weakened me.

39.11.0.en: Wilt thou trust him that he will bring in thy seed, and gather it into thy threshing floor? [12]

39.11.1.en: Man can entrust tame animals; he leaves a small boy to lead his donkey or his ox, and lays burdens on the donkey, and ties the ox to the arms of a plow led by a boy. But he does not entrust a rhinoceros to do such works, by bringing it to the harvest and laying the load on it.

39.12.0.en: 13 "The wing of the ostrich flaps. Is it a kind pinion, or plumage? 14 For she leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in the dust, 15 And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may tread upon them. 16 She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers: her labour is in vain without regret. 17 Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding. 18 What time she betakes herself on high, she laugheth at the horse and his rider.

39.12.1.en: The wing of the ostrich flaps.

39.12.2.en: Is it a kind pinion, or plumage? [13]

39.12.3.en: As for the ostrich, it is a very large bird that some call a winged camel. He who sees it flapping its great wings thinks that it is able to fly, and with surpassing speed, but with the size of its wings and the beauty of its plumage it is unable to fly.

39.12.4.en: *The wings of the ostrich are like the wings of the "heron" and the wings of the falcon; who can be ignorant how the heron and the falcon surpass the rest of the birds in the speed of their flight?

39.12.5.en: The ostrich has two wings resembling theirs, but not their speed of flight. For truly it cannot rise from the earth and practice true flight. So are all the hypocrites who pretend to the conduct of the righteous and have the same good appearance, but have no true good conduct. It is as if God says: You have the appearance of your wings, so you seem like one who can rise, but the weight of your conduct drags you down to the lowest depths.

39.12.6.en: The bodies of the falcon and the heron are small, but they are supported by dense wings. Therefore they fly swiftly because what weighs them down is little and what supports them for flight is much... The character of the chosen man is well indicated by the heron and the falcon. As long as the chosen live in this life they cannot be free of some sin, however small it may seem. But as long as what weighs them down is little in them, they have an abundance of the virtue of good work which lifts them to the heights.

39.13.0.en: For she leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in the dust [14].

39.13.1.en: With the beautiful plumage the ostrich has, she struts like the peacock in pride, but she acts in stupidity without wisdom. For neither her beauty nor the largeness of her size is joined with wisdom. She does not care for her young, for she exposes her eggs to danger. She does not hide in a secluded place to make herself a nest like the sparrow and the swallow (Ps 84:3), nor does she sit on the eggs until they hatch. She leaves her eggs on the ground anywhere, they can hatch by the warmth of the sun and the sand, and she does not trouble herself to warm them.

39.13.2.en: It is a painful picture of some believers who do not care for the salvation of their children, whether according to the flesh or those whom they have begotten in the Gospel, but leave them as in the dust of this world, yet the grace of God often seeks them and supports them with the warmth of the Sun of righteousness, so that they enjoy the risen life.

39.13.3.en: * To leave the eggs on the ground is not to care for the upbringing of the children they have begotten through conversion, by raising them above earthly work by giving counsel. To leave the eggs on the ground is not to support them by giving the children an example of the heavenly life.

39.13.4.en: What is meant by dust but the sinner...? What does dust indicate but the instability of the wicked? Therefore the Lord warms the eggs that are left in the dust, kindling the fire of His love for the little souls deprived of the earnest care of the preachers, even when they dwell among sinners.

39.14.0.en: And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may tread upon them! [15]

39.14.1.en: In stupidity the ostrich leaves her eggs in the dust, without considering that the foot of a man might tread on it or an animal might shatter it. Yet God in His love sends the heat of the sun to warm it until it hatches.

39.14.2.en: Pope Gregory in his symbolic interpretation sees that some preachers, after presenting to God children through their preaching, leave those who have accepted the faith as in the dust, in the midst of the wicked, and do not care about the trampling of feet to which they are exposed when the wicked try to discourage them, and when they are exposed to a beast of prey that shatters them, that is, to the trials of the wicked devil.

39.14.3.en: She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers.

39.15.0.en: Her labour is in vain without regret [16].

39.15.1.en: We are not surprised if the ostrich is hardened against her young as though they were not hers, so that all her labor is fruitless, in contrast to the majority of birds and animals that expose themselves to danger even to death for their young. But what surprises us is that the rational man ignores his children according to the flesh or the spirit, as though they were not his, and his whole life becomes tasteless.

39.15.2.en: * He who does not enjoy the grace of love looks at his neighbor as a stranger, even if he has begotten him for God.

39.15.3.en: What tender compassion Paul had when he ran for the sake of his children with the warmth of such great love: "(God) is my witness how without ceasing I make mention of you, always making request in my prayers, if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come unto you. For I long to see you" (Rom 1:9-11)... For he was not like the ostrich, forgetting her children, but he feared greatly for his disciples as they suffered persecutions during their preaching, making light of the faith... He counted the wounds of his body in him as nothing, for fear lest the hearts of his children be wounded.

39.16.0.en: Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding [17].

39.16.1.en: God permitted that the huge, beautiful ostrich should not enjoy wisdom, while the tiny ant, which we despise, enjoys it. He wished us to learn from both to seek wisdom and cherish it and practice it.

39.16.2.en: Since the ostrich represents the hypocritical person who has the beautiful, good appearance without the holy heart, she was not made worthy to receive wisdom.

39.16.3.en: For God in His love wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, offering wisdom to everyone who seeks it with sincerity and longing. But if we do not care for it, even natural wisdom is taken from us.

39.17.0.en: What time she betakes herself on high, she laugheth at the horse and his rider [18].

39.17.1.en: In spite of the ostrich's neglect of her young, when some danger encircles her she lifts her wings and sets off with surpassing speed, so that she mocks the horse and his rider.

39.17.2.en: * Let God be your hope, your ability to endure, your strength. Let Him be your atonement, your praise, your goal and resting place, and your help in your striving...

39.17.3.en: The mighty man is the arrogant man who exalts himself (in pride) against God, as though he were something in himself and what belongs to him. Such a man is not saved by his own strength.

39.17.4.en: Now, he has a nimble and strong horse, sound and swift of foot; if an attack takes place, can it not save its rider from the danger that surrounds him? Let him hear: "The salvation of the horse is a lie"... You must not let the horse promise you escape...

39.17.5.en: We can take the horse as a symbol of any possessions in this world, or of any kind of honor in which we trust in pride, counting mistakenly that the higher you rise the more your safety and your height increase. Do you not perceive with what violence you will be cast down; the higher you ascend, the heavier will be your fall... How then is safety achieved? It is not achieved by power nor by authority nor by honor nor by glory nor by the horse.

39.18.0.en: 19 "Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane? 20 Canst thou make him leap as a locust? The snorting of his nostrils is terrible. 21 He paweth in the valley, and leapeth with might. He goeth forth to meet the weapons. 22 He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword. 23 Against him the arrows rattle, with the point of the spear and the javelin. 24 In his leaping and his rumbling he devoureth the ground, neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet. 25 At the blast of the trumpet he saith, Aha! and from afar he scenteth the battle, the shouting of the captains and the cry.

39.18.1.en: Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane? [19]

39.18.2.en: After speaking of the wild animals and the birds of the wilderness, He presents to him as an example a tame animal serving man, the horse.

39.18.3.en: He asks him if horses are used to protect man in battles, who gave them the strength? It is not a gift from man, but from God. Yet he who depends on horses without looking to God the giver of strength loses the victory. The psalmist says: "An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength" (Ps 33:17), as it is said: "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse" (Ps 147:10; cf. Hos 14:3; Ps 20:7; Isa 31:1, 3).

39.18.4.en: Horses are used in Holy Scripture to carry many meanings, among them: 1. Reliance on temporal honor: "I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth" (Eccl 10:7). The servants here refer to the wicked enslaved to sin, who exalt themselves with temporal positions and vain honor.

39.18.5.en: b. It carries a good meaning, as it is said: "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:31). The horse here refers to the believer's abilities and powers that face the opposition of the devil and prevail through the work of God in them.

39.18.6.en: c. Horses also refer to the preachers: "Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters" (Hab 3:15).

39.18.7.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the horse in this place (Job 39:19) means the good preachers who win souls by God's work through them and in them.

39.18.8.en: With the strength a horse has, man relied on it to defend himself and his country and his possessions, yet a small boy can lead it without rebellion on its part.

39.19.0.en: Canst thou make him leap as a locust? The snorting of his nostrils is terrible [20].

39.19.1.en: God asks Job if he is able to hide him like a small locust, for the snorting of his nose in battles is terrifying! He attacks the enemy and does not fear danger to his life.

39.19.2.en: He paweth in the valley, and leapeth with might.

39.20.0.en: He goeth forth to meet the weapons [21].

39.20.1.en: He had previously spoken of the rhinoceros which by its strength mocks man and does not serve him, but here he presents the horse which with its great strength submits to man, and works in his service at the expense of its very life. It goes out to meet the weapons without fear of death!

39.20.2.en: The text in the Septuagint reads: "He paweth with his hoof in the plain, rejoicing." He is like one who seeks heavenly things, and strikes the earth with his hoof with all strength and boldness, not subject to the passions of his body. Truly Solomon the Wise says: "Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house" (Prov 24:27).

39.21.0.en: He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword [22].

39.22.0.en: Against him the arrows rattle, with the point of the spear (and the lance) and the javelin [23].

39.22.1.en: Out of loyalty to his master the horse laughs at death, and is not frightened by the attacks of the enemies, whether by sword or spear, and does not retreat but continues his advance into the midst of the battle, inspiring his rider with the spirit of courage!

39.22.2.en: Truly man stands in shame when he does not make light of death for the sake of his loyalty to and love for his Creator!

39.22.3.en: The Apostle Paul himself offers us a wonderful example of love unto death, when he says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" (Rom 8:35-36).

39.23.0.en: In his leaping and his anger he devoureth the ground (in his leaping and his rumbling he devoureth the ground), neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet [24].

39.23.1.en: If the horse in battle is full of zeal and enthusiasm and composure, devouring the ground, should not the believer in his spiritual battle be marked by courage and certainty of God's work with him?

39.23.2.en: "Neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet." What does this mean? When the apostles preached the Gospel, the high priest sounded the trumpet, not to work for the Lord, but to nullify the work of preaching the Kingdom. "And when they had called the apostles, and beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus" (Acts 5:40). But the apostles realized that this was not the sound of the true trumpet, so they said: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20).

39.23.3.en: At the blast of the trumpet he saith, Aha!

39.24.0.en: And from afar he scenteth the battle, the shouting of the captains and the cry [25].

39.24.1.en: * When (the believer) obtains the weapon of the Lord, then as soon as he hears of the existence of wars and feels them, he advances [with shouting and a cry] as it says in Job (Job 39:25), because the very voice of his prayer makes the enemies fall to the ground.

39.25.0.en: 26 "Doth the hawk take flight by thy understanding, and stretch his wings toward the south? 27 Or doth the eagle soar at thy command, and make his nest on high? 28 He dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the stronghold. 29 From thence he seeketh his food; his eyes behold afar off. 30 His young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is he."

39.25.1.en: Doth the hawk take flight by thy understanding, and stretch his wings toward the south? [26]

39.25.2.en: The hawk is marked by the speed of its flight and strength; it is among the birds of prey; it spreads its wings and flies toward the south, escaping from the cold regions in the north, especially when it sheds its feathers and replaces them with new feathers. Who gave it this wisdom but God?

39.25.3.en: * What then is the falcon(b) that enjoys its (new) plumage in the south but every saint who burns when touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, and so casts off the old habit of dialogue, and takes the form of the new man? Paul advises, saying: "Ye have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new" (Col 3:9-10). And also: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16).

39.25.4.en: To spread our wings toward the south means to open our hearts in confession, by the descent of the Holy Spirit, so that we no longer find our pleasure in hiding ourselves by defending ourselves, but expose ourselves by accusing ourselves.

39.25.6.en: * Who can distinguish the nature of the birds of the air?! How some of them enjoy melodious voices, and another is speckled with all colors in its wings, and some hover in the air as though motionless like the eagle. For by divine command "he (the hawk) stretcheth his wings toward the south." Who can see the lofty height of the falcon...?! How then do you wish to understand the Creator of all?!

39.26.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Or doth the eagle soar at thy command, and make his nest on high? [27]

39.26.1.en: The eagle - the king of birds - offers us an example of the mighty capacities that God gives even to this bird, as a symbol of the capacities of man, who can use them for building for the Kingdom of God within him and in the hearts of others, or for destruction and violence and predation.

39.26.2.en: Here the characteristics of the eagle stand out, and they are: 1. His soaring very high during his flight by the strength of his wings. Where did he get this ability, is it a gift from man to the eagle? But it is a natural instinct God gave him.

39.26.3.en: He who created the eagle among the birds for man's sake and gave him the ability to soar on high, will He not grant man to rise by the Holy Spirit of God to enjoy the flight toward the heavenly things?

39.26.4.en: The eagle uses flying high in order to be hidden from sight, and with the power of his vision and the swiftness of his movement he suddenly swoops upon the prey. So the wicked man uses the capacities offered to him to harm others instead of helping and supporting them. 2. He makes his nest in the high rocks on the crag of the rock, so that no one reaches his young.

39.27.0.en: He dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the stronghold [28].

39.27.1.en: It befits the believer to make his nest in Christ Jesus, the true Rock, so that evil does not approach him.

39.27.2.en: But he who in arrogance and pride exalts himself and thinks he has set up for himself a rock which no one approaches, and walks in evil securely, hears the voice: "Though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the LORD" (Jer 49:16). 3. The keenness of his sight: the believer's inner sight is opened to see the earnest of heaven and enjoy it. But the wicked uses the keenness of his sight to look downward, and his heart is full of violence and predation.

39.27.3.en: From thence he seeketh his food.

39.28.0.en: His eyes behold afar off [29]. 4. His young ones suck up blood from their youth and live with the great eagle on the prey.

39.29.0.en: His young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is he [30].

39.29.1.en: All thirst for the shedding of blood as their daily food. But the believers gather like holy eagles around the slain Lord Christ for the sake of their eternal resurrection. Christ becomes their spiritual food: "For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together" (Mt 24:28).

39.29.2.en: * In Holy Scripture the word eagle sometimes refers to spiteful spirits, corrupters of souls; and sometimes to the powers of the present world. But at times it refers to the sharp understanding of the saints, or to the incarnate Lord, flying swiftly above lower things and seeking the things above.

39.29.3.en: Jeremiah bears witness to the spirits resting in expectation: "Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven" (Lam 4:19)... It also symbolizes earthly power, as it was said by the prophet Ezekiel: "A great eagle, large of wings, long of pinions, broad of shoulders, full of splendors, came unto Lebanon, and took the branch of the cedar, he cropped off the top of its young twigs" (Ezek 17:3-4). For this eagle in truth to whom does it point but Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon...?

39.29.4.en: By the word "eagle" is indicated the sharp understanding of the saints, or the flight of Christ's ascension. Therefore the same prophet (Ezekiel), in describing the four Evangelists whom he saw under the appearance of living creatures, declared that they appeared to him in the form of the face of a man and a lion and an ox and an eagle; he surely indicated by the eagle the fourth living creature, John, who in his flight left the earth, and through sharp understanding penetrated inner mysteries by his vision of the Word...

39.29.5.en: Let us look at the very structure of the eagle, the nest of hope in heavenly things. Paul says: "For our conversation is in heaven" (Phil 3:20). And also: "And hath raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him in heavenly places" (Eph 2:6)... For as he who climbs a mountain looks downward and sees lower things as small, so the more a man advances to higher stages, striving to fix his care on the heavenly things, he finds with the same effort that the glory of the present life is nothing, and rises above the places of the earth.

39.29.7.en: Your creation calls me to meet You!

39.29.8.en: * For my sake You created the earth and all that is on it.

39.29.9.en: Behold, even the animals and the birds call me to meet You!

39.29.10.en: Grant me, with the wild goats of the rocks, to run to You, and to hide in You, O Rock of Ages.

39.29.11.en: * Grant me, with the hinds, to thirst for You.

39.29.12.en: That I may strike with You the head of the serpent.

39.29.13.en: And the devil shall not have dominion over me.

39.29.14.en: By You I crush him, for You cast him down from heaven like lightning, and though he appears luminous, it is only for a moment, and his deceit is exposed.

39.29.15.en: * Grant me to be a fruitful hind.

39.29.16.en: That I may bring forth for You children by the Gospel!

39.29.17.en: It is Your work, O Shepherd of all!

39.29.18.en: * Let me learn even from the wild ass the freedom of the wilderness.

39.29.19.en: Why should I confine myself in the animals' stall?

39.29.20.en: Let me go forth to the wilderness of the Spirit, and let my soul fly to You with joy and exultation.

39.29.21.en: * I see the rhinoceros, and my soul trembles at falling into pride.

39.29.22.en: Why should I be arrogant about the strength and abilities and gifts You have given me?

39.29.23.en: Why do I not commit myself, in a spirit of humility, to draw near to the manger?

39.29.24.en: You are the food of my soul.

39.29.25.en: You are my satisfaction and my joy!

39.29.26.en: * I see the beautiful, huge ostrich, and I fear that I may be occupied with outward appearances without the wisdom of the Spirit.

39.29.27.en: I fear that I may act in stupidity and leave the little ones in the dust.

39.29.28.en: And not offer the weak the warmth of love and the power of the Spirit!

39.29.29.en: * Count me as a holy horse, bearing You in my heart, O unique Rider.

39.29.30.en: I do not fear spiritual battles, nor take account of the death of the body.

39.29.31.en: I am not troubled by the enemy's spears, nor do I fear the sword of the devil!

39.29.32.en: By You I prevail and am crowned!

39.29.33.en: * Let me renew my plumage always with the falcon.

39.29.34.en: I put off always the old man and all his deeds, and put on always the new man.

39.29.35.en: May he be renewed every day by the work of Your Holy Spirit.

39.29.36.en: Let me sing to You, saying:

39.29.37.en: Behold, all things have become new!

39.29.38.en: * Let me fly with the eagle in the heavenly places.

39.29.39.en: Let my depths soar to the earnest of eternity.

39.29.40.en: Let the eyes of my heart look to the crowns prepared.

39.29.41.en: Let me throw myself into Your arms and live by You and with You!
